author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Can machines be creative?
standfirst: Software can now write poems, compose music and produce images in seconds. Whether that counts as creativity depends on what we think creativity is.
paragraphs: [A] Not long ago, creativity was often described as the one thing machines would never be able to do. Computers could calculate faster than any human and beat champions at chess, but writing a moving story or painting an original picture seemed to require something uniquely human. Today, generative software can produce essays, songs and illustrations on request, and the old certainty has disappeared.

[B] These systems work by analysing enormous quantities of existing text, images or sound and learning the statistical patterns within them. When asked to produce something new, they generate output that follows those patterns. The results can be impressive: fluent, stylish and, at times, genuinely surprising. Yet critics argue that recombining what already exists, however skilfully, is not the same as creating.

[C] Defenders reply that human creativity also builds on what came before. Writers absorb the books they have read; composers borrow forms and harmonies from their predecessors. Very few ideas appear from nowhere. On this view, the difference between human and machine creativity is one of degree rather than kind.

[D] Psychologists often define creativity as producing something that is both novel and valuable. Machines can clearly produce novelty. Value is harder, because it depends on judgement: someone must decide that a piece of work is meaningful, beautiful or useful. At present, that judgement still comes from people, who choose the prompts, select among many outputs and decide what to keep.

[E] The rise of these tools has also raised practical concerns. Artists and authors have asked whether their work was used to train systems without their permission, and courts in several countries are considering how copyright law applies. Teachers worry about students submitting machine-written essays, while some employers see opportunities to cut costs in design and marketing.

[F] Perhaps the most useful question is not whether machines are creative, but how they change human creativity. Like photography in the nineteenth century, which pushed painters away from realism and towards new styles, generative tools may push people towards the kinds of work that depend most on personal experience, intention and taste.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Should voting be compulsory?
standfirst: In a few democracies, citizens can be fined for not voting. Is that a strength of democracy or a contradiction of it?
paragraphs: [A] In most democracies, voting is a right that citizens are free to use or ignore. In a minority of countries, including Australia, Belgium and several in Latin America, it is also a legal duty. Australia introduced compulsory voting for federal elections in the 1920s, and turnout there regularly exceeds ninety per cent, far higher than in many countries where voting is voluntary.

[B] Supporters argue that compulsory voting produces governments that represent the whole population rather than the most motivated part of it. Where voting is optional, turnout is often lowest among younger, poorer and less educated citizens, so politicians have an incentive to focus on older, wealthier groups who reliably vote. Requiring everyone to participate, the argument goes, forces parties to appeal to the centre and to address the concerns of people they might otherwise ignore.

[C] There are practical benefits too. Parties spend less money persuading their supporters to turn up and can concentrate on persuading undecided voters. Some researchers also suggest that compulsory systems reduce the influence of extreme views, because the electorate is broader than the activists who dominate low-turnout elections.

[D] Opponents see a fundamental contradiction: a democracy that compels people to take part is restricting the very freedom it claims to protect. Choosing not to vote, they argue, can itself be a political statement. Others worry that forcing uninterested citizens to vote adds random or uninformed choices to the result. In practice, most compulsory systems require only that people attend or return a ballot; they may still spoil it or leave it blank.

[E] The penalties involved are usually small fines, and enforcement varies. What seems to matter most is the norm: once voting is expected of everyone, it becomes a habit, and many citizens in such countries say they would continue to vote even if the law changed. Whether that habit could be created elsewhere without compulsion remains an open question.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: The fifteen-minute city
standfirst: What if everything you needed each day were within a short walk or bike ride? An idea from urban planning has become a political flashpoint.
paragraphs: [A] The concept is easy to state. In a fifteen-minute city, residents can reach most of their everyday needs, including work, schools, shops, healthcare and green space, within a quarter of an hour on foot or by bicycle. The idea, popularised in the late 2010s by the academic Carlos Moreno and adopted by the mayor of Paris, draws on much older traditions of compact, mixed-use neighbourhoods.

[B] For most of the twentieth century, planners in many countries did the opposite. Homes, offices and shopping areas were separated into different zones and connected by roads. This model suited the car, but it also meant long commutes, heavy traffic and town centres that emptied after office hours. Supporters of the fifteen-minute city argue that reversing this separation would cut emissions, improve health and strengthen local communities.

[C] In practice, the changes are often modest. Schoolyards may be opened to the public at weekends, streets near schools closed to cars at certain times, cycle lanes added and planning rules adjusted so that small shops and clinics can open in residential areas. None of this prevents anyone from driving; it aims to make driving less necessary.

[D] Nevertheless, the idea has attracted fierce opposition. Some critics see it as a disguised attempt to restrict personal freedom, especially when it is combined with traffic-control schemes that limit car access to certain streets. Others raise more practical objections: in sprawling suburbs and rural areas, the density needed to support local services simply does not exist, and building it would take decades.

[E] There are also concerns about fairness. If a neighbourhood becomes more pleasant to live in, property prices may rise, pushing out the lower-income residents the plan was supposed to help. Planners therefore increasingly argue that the fifteen-minute city must be accompanied by affordable housing policies.

[F] Much of the controversy may come from the name, which sounds like a rule rather than an aspiration. Few supporters claim that every city can be redesigned within fifteen-minute boundaries. The underlying question is more basic: should cities be planned primarily around cars, or around the people who live in them?

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Governing the commons: why tragedy is not inevitable
standfirst: For decades, economists assumed that shared resources were doomed to be overused unless the state or the market took control. Elinor Ostrom spent her career showing that communities often do better.
paragraphs: [A] Imagine a pasture open to every herder in a village. Each herder gains the full benefit of adding one more animal, while the cost of overgrazing is shared among everyone. The individually rational choice, repeated by each herder, leads to a collectively disastrous result: the grass is destroyed and all are ruined. This parable, popularised in a 1968 essay as "the tragedy of the commons", became one of the most influential ideas in environmental thinking. It seemed to explain overfishing, deforestation and the depletion of groundwater with unsettling clarity.

[B] The policy conclusion appeared equally clear. If individuals cannot be trusted to restrain themselves, shared resources must either be placed under the control of the state, which can impose limits, or divided into private property, so that each owner bears the cost of his or her own overuse. For much of the twentieth century these two options — government regulation or privatisation — framed almost every debate about natural resources.

[C] The political scientist Elinor Ostrom challenged this dichotomy not with a rival theory but with evidence. Studying fisheries, forests, irrigation systems and mountain pastures in many parts of the world, she and her colleagues documented communities that had managed shared resources sustainably, in some cases for centuries, without relying on either a central authority or private ownership. In 2009 she became the first woman to receive the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, awarded for her analysis of economic governance, especially the commons.

[D] What distinguished the successful cases was not altruism but institutions: rules, often unwritten, that the users themselves had devised and enforced. Ostrom identified recurring features. The boundaries of the resource and the group entitled to use it were clearly defined. Rules were adapted to local conditions and could be modified by the people affected. Users monitored one another, and sanctions for breaking the rules were graduated, starting mildly and escalating for repeat offenders. Cheap and accessible mechanisms existed for resolving disputes, and external authorities recognised the community's right to organise itself.

[E] These findings did not overturn the tragedy of the commons so much as qualify it. The original parable assumes that herders cannot communicate or make binding agreements. Where those conditions hold — among strangers, for instance, or when a resource is too vast for anyone to monitor — overuse remains a real danger. Ostrom's point was that such conditions are an empirical question rather than a law of nature, and that well-meaning interventions which replace functioning local arrangements with distant regulation or hasty privatisation can destroy the very trust on which cooperation depends.

[F] The relevance of her work has, if anything, grown. Many of the most pressing problems of the present — climate change, the oceans, even shared digital infrastructure — are commons on a global scale, where the features that made small communities successful are hardest to reproduce. Ostrom herself warned against "panaceas", single solutions applied regardless of context. Her legacy is less a formula than a disposition: a willingness to look at how people actually cooperate before deciding that they cannot.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: The long journey of a cheap T-shirt
standfirst: A simple cotton T-shirt may cross several borders before it reaches a shop. Following its journey reveals how the global economy really works.
paragraphs: [A] Few products seem as ordinary as a plain cotton T-shirt. Yet the one you are wearing may have travelled further than you have this year. Its cotton might have been grown in one country, spun into yarn in a second, knitted and dyed in a third, sewn in a fourth and finally shipped to a warehouse in a fifth before being sold online.

[B] This long supply chain exists because each stage is carried out wherever it is cheapest or most efficient. Cotton grows best in warm climates with plenty of water or irrigation. Spinning and weaving are highly mechanised, so they tend to be located where energy is cheap and factories are large. Sewing, by contrast, still depends heavily on human hands, and is therefore concentrated in countries where wages are low.

[C] Supporters of globalisation argue that this division of labour has made clothing far more affordable and created millions of jobs in developing economies. For many workers, often young women moving from rural areas, a factory job offers a regular income and a degree of independence that farming did not. Several countries have used the garment industry as a first step towards more advanced manufacturing.

[D] The costs, however, are significant. Wages in the sewing stage are frequently barely enough to live on, and working conditions vary widely. Serious factory accidents have drawn international attention to unsafe buildings and weak inspections. The environmental impact is also considerable: growing cotton can require large amounts of water and pesticides, dyeing can pollute rivers, and transporting goods across oceans adds to carbon emissions.

[E] Consumers increasingly ask where their clothes come from, and many brands now publish lists of their suppliers or join certification schemes. Critics warn, though, that transparency at the top of the chain does not always reach the subcontractors further down, where problems are hardest to see. Others argue that the most effective change would come from buying fewer, longer-lasting clothes, an idea that sits uncomfortably with the business model of fast fashion.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: The quiet health risk of loneliness
standfirst: Doctors increasingly treat loneliness not just as a sad feeling, but as a public health problem.
paragraphs: [A] Loneliness is usually discussed as an emotional experience, something painful but private. Over the past two decades, however, researchers have built up evidence that persistent loneliness is also associated with physical health problems, including heart disease, weakened immunity and a higher risk of dementia in older age. Some public health bodies now describe it as a risk factor comparable to well-known lifestyle risks.

[B] It is important to distinguish loneliness from being alone. Many people live by themselves and feel perfectly content, while others feel isolated in a busy family or office. Loneliness is the gap between the social connection a person wants and the connection they actually have. That is why it can affect people of any age, including students who have just left home and young parents at home with a baby.

[C] Why should a feeling damage the body? One explanation is that humans evolved in groups, where being cut off from others was genuinely dangerous. Chronic loneliness may keep the body in a state of mild alarm, raising stress hormones and disturbing sleep. Lonely people may also be less likely to exercise, eat well or seek medical help, because no one encourages them to do so.

[D] Responses have taken several forms. In some countries, doctors can now refer patients to community activities, such as walking groups, choirs or volunteering, a practice sometimes called social prescribing. Cities have experimented with benches where strangers are invited to talk, and with housing schemes that mix students and older residents. A few governments have even appointed a minister with responsibility for loneliness.

[E] Technology is an ambiguous part of the picture. Video calls and online communities can keep people in touch across distances, and were a lifeline for many during periods of lockdown. Yet heavy use of social media has been linked with feelings of isolation in some studies, perhaps because comparing ourselves with others' carefully edited lives makes our own seem empty.

[F] There is no single cure, partly because loneliness has so many causes. But recognising it as a health issue, rather than a personal weakness, may make it easier for people to admit that they are struggling, and that may be the first step towards reconnecting.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Measuring what matters: the case for looking beyond GDP
standfirst: Gross domestic product is the most watched number in economics. Its critics argue that it was never meant to measure how well people live.
paragraphs: [A] When politicians boast about a growing economy, they are almost always referring to gross domestic product: the total value of goods and services produced in a country over a period of time. GDP is an extraordinarily useful statistic. It allows comparisons between countries and across decades, and changes in it signal booms and recessions. But it is also routinely treated as something it was never designed to be: a measure of national well-being.

[B] The limitations are well known to economists. GDP counts market activity, so unpaid work such as caring for children or elderly relatives does not appear in it, however valuable it is. It records spending without asking what the spending is for: rebuilding after a flood or treating the victims of pollution adds to GDP just as building a new school does. It says nothing about how income is distributed, so an economy can grow while most households see no improvement. And it treats the depletion of forests, fisheries and fossil fuels as income rather than as the running down of a stock of natural wealth.

[C] None of these criticisms is new. Robert F. Kennedy famously criticised the measure in a 1968 speech, and the debate gained official momentum when the French government set up a commission led by the economists Joseph Stiglitz, Amartya Sen and Jean-Paul Fitoussi. Its 2009 report argued that over-reliance on GDP had given policymakers a distorted picture, and recommended a broader "dashboard" of indicators covering material living standards, health, education, inequality, security, social connections, the environment and people's own evaluations of their lives.

[D] Since then, the "beyond GDP" agenda has moved from academic discussion into official statistics. The OECD launched its Better Life Initiative, and a follow-up report by an expert group linked to the original commission argued that focusing on the wrong indicators had contributed to inadequate policy responses to the 2008 financial crisis. National statistical offices now publish measures of well-being alongside traditional economic data, and the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals set targets that go well beyond output.

[E] Critics of the dashboard approach raise practical objections. A single number is easy to communicate and hard to manipulate; dozens of indicators can be selectively quoted, and governments may highlight whichever ones look favourable. Combining very different dimensions — life expectancy, air quality, trust in institutions — into a single index requires value judgements about their relative importance, and reasonable people disagree. Subjective measures such as life satisfaction may also be influenced by culture and by how questions are asked.

[F] The defenders of broader measurement rarely argue that GDP should be abolished. Their point is about attention. As Stiglitz has put it, what we measure affects what we do. If a government is judged mainly by growth, it will pursue growth, even when the costs fall on health, nature or future generations. A richer set of indicators cannot settle political arguments about what matters most, but it can ensure that those arguments are conducted with the full picture in view.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Letting nature take back control
standfirst: Rewilding promises to restore damaged ecosystems by doing less, not more. But who decides what "wild" should look like?
paragraphs: [A] For most of the twentieth century, conservation meant management. Reserves were fenced, grass was cut, invasive plants were removed and particular species were protected, often at considerable expense. Rewilding takes a strikingly different approach. Its central idea is that, given enough space and a few key ingredients, natural processes can repair ecosystems more effectively than human planning can.

[B] The most famous example is the return of grey wolves to Yellowstone National Park in the United States in the mid-1990s, after an absence of about seventy years. Supporters argue that the wolves did far more than reduce the number of elk. Because the elk began to avoid open valleys where they were vulnerable, young trees along riverbanks had a chance to grow. Their roots stabilised the banks, and new habitats appeared for birds and beavers. Scientists call such a chain of effects a trophic cascade, although some researchers now believe the Yellowstone story has been simplified, and that drought, hunting and other factors also played a part.

[C] In Europe, rewilding has taken a different form, partly because large predators and dense human populations are an uneasy combination. Projects have reintroduced beavers, whose dams slow down rivers and reduce flooding downstream, and grazing animals such as wild cattle and horses, which keep landscapes open in a more varied way than mowing. In some regions, farmland abandoned as rural populations decline has simply been left to recover on its own.

[D] Critics raise several objections. Farmers worry about livestock losses when predators return, and compensation schemes are not always generous or quick. Others question whether there is any meaningful "natural" state to return to, since landscapes have been shaped by people for thousands of years. Choosing a baseline, whether before industrialisation, before farming or before humans arrived, is ultimately a value judgement rather than a scientific fact.

[E] There are economic arguments on both sides as well. Rewilded areas can attract tourists and create jobs in guiding and hospitality, sometimes in regions where agriculture is no longer profitable. Yet these benefits rarely reach everyone equally, and residents who depended on traditional land use may feel that decisions are being made by distant organisations with little understanding of local life.

[F] Perhaps the most persuasive case for rewilding is a modest one. It does not claim that nature can solve every environmental problem, nor that human management is always harmful. Instead, it suggests that, in the right places, stepping back may achieve more than intervening. The challenge is to decide, together with the people who live there, where those places are.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Second lives: why cities are reusing old buildings
standfirst: Demolishing an old building and starting again used to be the obvious choice. Increasingly, architects argue that the greenest building is the one that already exists.
paragraphs: [A] For most of the twentieth century, cities treated old industrial buildings as obstacles. Factories, warehouses and power stations that had lost their original purpose were usually demolished, and something new was built in their place. Today the opposite approach, known as adaptive reuse, is becoming mainstream. Instead of knocking a building down, designers keep its structure and give it a new function: a mill becomes flats, a railway shed becomes a market, a church becomes a library.

[B] One of the best-known examples is in London. Bankside Power Station, designed by Sir Giles Gilbert Scott and built in stages after the Second World War, stopped generating electricity in 1981 and stood empty for years, regularly threatened with demolition. In the mid-1990s the Tate gallery chose it as the home for a new museum of modern art, and the Swiss architects Herzog & de Meuron converted it. Tate Modern opened in 2000. The huge turbine hall, once filled with machinery, became a public space for large installations, and the building's industrial character became part of its appeal rather than something to hide.

[C] The environmental argument for reuse is simple but often overlooked. When we think about the carbon footprint of a building, we usually think about the energy needed to heat, cool and light it. However, a large share of a building's lifetime emissions comes from producing materials such as cement and steel and from construction itself. This so-called embodied carbon is released before anyone moves in. Demolishing a sound structure throws that investment away and creates waste, while a new building must "pay back" its own embodied carbon over many years before it becomes more efficient than the one it replaced.

[D] There are social reasons, too. Familiar buildings give neighbourhoods a sense of continuity and identity. Residents who have watched a local landmark decay often feel strongly about what happens to it, and successful projects frequently start with community campaigns. Reused buildings can also offer qualities that are expensive to create from scratch: high ceilings, thick walls, large windows and generous spaces that suit studios, schools and workplaces.

[E] Adaptive reuse is not always straightforward, however. Old buildings may contain hazardous materials, fail modern fire and accessibility standards, or be poorly insulated. Converting them can be technically complex and, in some cases, more expensive than building new. There is also the question of what to keep. Designers must decide which features carry the building's character and which can be changed, and conservation rules may limit their choices. Critics point out that celebrated conversions sometimes attract wealthier newcomers, contributing to rising rents in surrounding areas.

[F] Despite these challenges, many architects now argue that demolition should be the last option rather than the first. Some cities ask developers to justify why an existing building cannot be adapted before permission to demolish it is granted. The question is shifting from "Is this building worth saving?" to "Can we afford not to save it?" For a profession under pressure to cut emissions, the most sustainable material may be the one that is already standing.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Why we forget, and how to remember
standfirst: More than a century ago, a German psychologist tested his own memory with nonsense syllables. His findings still shape how good learners study today.
paragraphs: [A] In the 1880s, the psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus set himself an unusual task. He memorised long lists of meaningless syllables, such as "DAX" or "ZUF", and then tested how many he could still recall after different intervals. Using nonsense was deliberate: real words carry associations that make some easier to remember than others, and he wanted to measure memory in its purest form.

[B] What he found has become known as the forgetting curve. Memory loss was steepest at the beginning. Within an hour, a large part of a newly learned list had gone; after a day, more had disappeared; but after that, forgetting slowed down considerably. What remained after a week tended to stay. The exact figures varied with the material, yet the shape of the curve, a sharp drop followed by a long, flat tail, has been confirmed by researchers many times since.

[C] Ebbinghaus also noticed something more encouraging. When he relearned a list he had partly forgotten, it took him less time than the first attempt. The memory had not vanished completely; it had merely become harder to reach. Each time he reviewed the material, the curve that followed was flatter, meaning he forgot more slowly. This is the principle behind what is now called spaced repetition: rather than studying something many times in one session, you return to it at increasing intervals, ideally just before you would otherwise forget it.

[D] Later research added a second insight. Simply rereading notes feels productive, but it is a relatively weak way to learn. Testing yourself, by trying to recall an answer before checking it, strengthens memory far more. Psychologists call this retrieval practice. The effort of pulling information out of memory seems to be exactly what makes it stick. Ironically, the strategies that feel easiest, such as highlighting or rereading, often create an illusion of mastery, while the ones that feel difficult produce more durable learning.

[E] None of this means that cramming never works. A student who studies intensively the night before an exam may well pass it. The problem is what happens afterwards. Material crammed into a single session tends to follow the steep part of the forgetting curve, so much of it is lost within days. For anything that needs to last, such as a language, a professional skill or the foundations of a degree, spacing and self-testing are considerably more efficient.

[F] Digital tools have made these ideas easy to apply. Flashcard apps can calculate when each item is due for review, showing difficult words more often and easy ones less. But the underlying advice requires no technology at all: study a little, leave a gap, test yourself, and come back. Ebbinghaus's lists of nonsense, it turns out, contained a lesson that makes a great deal of sense.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Less work, same pay? The case for a four-day week
standfirst: Trials of a shorter working week have produced eye-catching results. Whether they can work everywhere is another question.
paragraphs: [A] For most of the last century, the five-day, forty-hour week has been treated as a natural law of working life. Yet it is a relatively recent invention. In many industrial countries, six-day weeks and far longer hours were normal until campaigns by trade unions and changes in technology gradually reduced them. Supporters of a four-day week argue that the next step is overdue.

[B] In recent years, companies in several countries have taken part in organised trials in which employees worked four days for the same pay, on condition that productivity remained stable. Many participating firms reported that output held steady or even improved, while staff described lower stress, better sleep and more time for family. A large proportion of the companies chose to continue the arrangement after the trial ended.

[C] Why might working less not mean producing less? One explanation is that much of the working week is not spent productively at all. Long meetings, unnecessary emails and constant interruptions fill hours without adding much value. When time is limited, teams tend to cut these first. Another explanation is that rested workers make fewer mistakes and are less likely to take sick leave, which reduces hidden costs for employers.

[D] Sceptics point out that the trials have important limitations. Companies volunteered to take part, so they were probably those most likely to succeed. Many were small firms in office-based sectors such as marketing or software, where output is harder to measure and work can be reorganised relatively easily. It is much less obvious how a hospital, a school or a factory running continuous shifts could cut a day without hiring more staff.

[E] There are also questions about fairness. If office workers gain an extra day off while nurses, drivers and shop assistants do not, existing divisions in the labour market could widen. Some economists suggest that, rather than a fixed four-day week for everyone, the real lesson of the trials is that working time should be more flexible and focused on results rather than hours.

[F] What seems clear is that the debate has moved from whether shorter hours are possible to how and where they make sense. As automation takes over more routine tasks, the question of how the gains are shared, through higher wages, lower prices or more free time, is likely to become one of the defining economic arguments of the coming decades.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: What will we eat for protein?
standfirst: Feeding a growing population without overheating the planet may require rethinking where our protein comes from.
paragraphs: [A] Meat and dairy are central to many diets, and demand for them tends to rise as countries become wealthier. Yet livestock farming uses a large share of the world's agricultural land and is responsible for a significant proportion of greenhouse gas emissions, especially methane from cattle. As the global population grows, scientists, companies and governments are looking for alternatives.

[B] The most familiar option is plant-based protein. Beans, lentils, chickpeas and soya have fed people for thousands of years and require far less land and water than beef. In recent years, food companies have used them to create products designed to imitate the taste and texture of meat. Sales grew quickly at first, but in several markets they have since levelled off, partly because of price and partly because some consumers are wary of heavily processed ingredients.

[C] A more radical approach is cultivated meat, grown from animal cells in large steel tanks rather than taken from slaughtered animals. Its supporters argue that it could provide real meat with a fraction of the land use and without animal suffering. Major challenges remain, however, including the cost of production at scale and the energy required to run the facilities. Only a few countries have so far approved its sale.

[D] Insects are another candidate. In many parts of the world, crickets, grasshoppers and larvae are already eaten as ordinary food, and they convert feed into protein very efficiently. In countries where insects are not traditionally eaten, the main obstacle is cultural rather than nutritional: many people simply find the idea unpleasant. Ground into flour and added to pasta or snacks, insects may become more acceptable.

[E] Most experts agree that no single solution will replace conventional meat. A more realistic future may combine several: eating smaller amounts of higher-quality meat, more traditional plant foods, and new products where they prove affordable and safe. As with many environmental questions, the challenge is as much about habits and culture as about technology.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: The marshmallow test revisited: what waiting really predicts
standfirst: A famous experiment seemed to show that a child's ability to wait for a treat shaped their future. A larger study told a more complicated story.
paragraphs: [A] Few psychology experiments are as well known as the "marshmallow test". In studies run at Stanford University from the 1960s, the psychologist Walter Mischel and his colleagues offered young children a choice: they could eat one treat immediately, or wait alone in a room for several minutes and receive two. Some children ate the treat almost at once; others sang, covered their eyes or turned away to resist temptation. Follow-up studies years later reported that children who had waited longer tended to have better outcomes as adolescents, including higher test scores.

[B] The findings became a cultural phenomenon. They were cited in books on success, in parenting advice and in school programmes designed to teach self-control. The appeal was obvious. The idea that a single, simple measure of willpower in early childhood could predict later achievement suggested a clear lesson: teach children to delay gratification, and their futures will improve.

[C] Scientists, however, had long been aware of the limitations of the original follow-ups. The samples were small and drawn largely from the children of staff and students at a prestigious university, a group far from representative of the wider population. In 2018, Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan published a conceptual replication in the journal Psychological Science. Using data from a much larger and more diverse group of children, they examined whether the ability to wait at around the age of four predicted achievement at fifteen.

[D] They did find an association, but it was considerably weaker than earlier work had suggested. More importantly, once they took into account factors such as family background, early cognitive ability and the home environment, the link shrank substantially. In other words, a child's ability to wait seemed to reflect, at least in part, the circumstances in which the child was growing up. A child from a household where promises are reliably kept has good reason to trust that a second treat will arrive; a child from a less predictable environment may reasonably take what is on offer now.

[E] It would be a mistake to conclude that self-control is irrelevant. Other research continues to find links between self-regulation and later outcomes, and some replications have reported that the marshmallow test retains a degree of predictive value. The more modest lesson concerns interpretation. A behaviour that looks like a fixed personal trait may partly be a rational response to the environment. Interventions that focus only on training individual willpower may therefore have less effect than those that address the conditions shaping children's choices.

[F] The story of the marshmallow test also illustrates how science is supposed to work. A striking result attracts attention; later researchers test it with better data; the conclusion is refined. The problem lies less with the original scientists than with the way their findings travelled beyond the laboratory, losing their caveats along the way. By the time the result reached popular culture, a cautious correlation had become a confident law of human destiny.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: The moral machine: can ethics be crowdsourced?
standfirst: An online experiment collected tens of millions of decisions about who a self-driving car should save in an unavoidable crash. Its results are fascinating. Whether they should guide engineers is another matter.
paragraphs: [A] Philosophers have long used the "trolley problem" to probe moral intuitions. A runaway tram will kill five people unless you divert it onto a track where it will kill one. Should you intervene? For decades the scenario was a classroom puzzle. The prospect of autonomous vehicles has turned it, at least in the eyes of some researchers, into an engineering question: if a crash is unavoidable, whom should a self-driving car be programmed to protect?

[B] To explore public attitudes, a team led by researchers at the MIT Media Lab built the Moral Machine, a multilingual online platform that presented visitors with dilemmas of this kind. Should the car swerve to spare pedestrians at the cost of its passengers? Should it favour the young over the old, the many over the few, people crossing legally over those crossing against the signal? The platform gathered some forty million decisions from millions of participants in more than two hundred countries and territories, and the results were published in Nature in 2018.

[C] Some preferences were remarkably consistent across the world: respondents tended to favour sparing humans over animals, more lives over fewer, and younger people over older ones. Other preferences varied considerably. The researchers identified broad clusters of countries whose answers differed in systematic ways, and found that some of these differences correlated with cultural and institutional characteristics, such as the strength of the rule of law or the degree of economic inequality.

[D] The study's authors presented their findings as a contribution to public debate, not as a set of instructions. Even so, the experiment raises difficult questions about the relationship between what people prefer and what is right. A majority preference is not, in itself, a moral justification; history offers many examples of widely shared views that are now regarded as unjust. Some preferences revealed by such surveys — for instance, valuing certain categories of people over others — would conflict with principles of equal treatment embedded in law in many countries. Germany's ethics commission on automated driving, for example, recommended that systems should not distinguish between people on the basis of personal features such as age.

[E] Critics also question whether the scenarios capture anything real. In practice, a vehicle facing an emergency rarely has certain knowledge of the outcomes of each option; it must act under uncertainty, in fractions of a second, with imperfect sensors. Engineers point out that most safety gains come not from resolving dramatic dilemmas but from avoiding them altogether — through cautious speeds, better braking and more reliable detection. On this view, the trolley problem is a distraction that makes machine ethics seem more exotic, and more tractable, than it is.

[F] Yet the experiment's value may lie precisely in what it exposes. Automated systems will embody choices about risk, whether or not those choices are made explicit. Somebody decides how cautiously a car should drive near a school, how it should balance the safety of its occupants against that of cyclists, and who bears responsibility when it fails. Crowdsourcing cannot settle these questions. What it can do is show how differently people answer them, and remind us that leaving the decisions to engineers alone is itself a moral choice.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: The planes that came back: survivorship bias in business advice
standfirst: Success stories are everywhere, and most of them teach the wrong lesson. A wartime puzzle explains why.
paragraphs: [A] During the Second World War, military planners faced a difficult question. Bombers returning from missions were full of bullet holes, and adding armour could save lives. But armour is heavy, so it could not be added everywhere. The obvious solution was to reinforce the areas where the returning aircraft had been hit most often. A statistician called Abraham Wald, working for a research group in New York, is widely credited with pointing out the flaw in this reasoning.

[B] The planes being examined were only the ones that had survived. Aircraft hit in other places, such as the engines, had not come back at all, so their damage never appeared in the data. The holes on the returning planes showed where a plane could be hit and still fly home. The armour, Wald argued, should go where the survivors had no holes. The story is often simplified in retelling, but the principle it illustrates has a name: survivorship bias, the error of drawing conclusions only from cases that made it through a selection process.

[C] Business advice is particularly vulnerable to this error. Bookshops are full of biographies of successful founders, and online articles analyse the morning routines of billionaires. The message is usually that their habits explain their success: they took bold risks, dropped out of university, or trusted their instincts. What these stories leave out is the much larger group of people who did exactly the same things and failed. Their companies closed quietly, and nobody wrote a book about them.

[D] Once you notice the bias, it appears everywhere. If we study only companies that have lasted a hundred years, we may conclude that their culture made them resilient, without knowing whether many failed firms had the same culture. Investment funds that performed badly are often closed or merged, so the average performance of the funds that remain looks better than the true average. Even the belief that old buildings were "built to last" may partly reflect the fact that badly built ones have already been demolished.

[E] None of this means that successful people have nothing to teach us. The problem is the method, not the source. To learn what causes success, we need to compare winners with losers who started from similar positions. Researchers try to do this by following a whole group over time, including those who drop out, rather than looking backwards from the end. In practical terms, it means asking an awkward question whenever we hear an inspiring story: how many people did the same thing and are not here to tell us about it?

[F] That question is uncomfortable because it removes some of the magic from success. It suggests that luck, timing and starting conditions matter more than many stories admit. But it also offers a kind of protection. A founder who understands survivorship bias is less likely to bet everything on a strategy simply because it worked for someone famous, and more likely to look for evidence that includes the failures.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: The power to attract: soft power in international relations
standfirst: Armies and economies are not the only sources of influence. A concept coined at the end of the Cold War asks why some countries get what they want simply by being admired — and whether that is really power at all.
paragraphs: [A] Power, in its most familiar form, is the ability to make others do what they would not otherwise do. States have traditionally exercised it through coercion — the threat or use of force — and through inducement, such as trade deals, aid and sanctions. At the end of the Cold War, the Harvard political scientist Joseph Nye argued that this picture was incomplete. There was a third way to obtain the outcomes one wants: to make others want the same outcomes. He called it soft power.

[B] Soft power, in Nye's account, rests on attraction rather than pressure. Its resources are a country's culture, where others find it appealing; its political values, when it lives up to them at home and abroad; and its foreign policies, when others regard them as legitimate. A state whose universities draw students from around the world, whose films and music are widely enjoyed, and whose institutions are admired may find that other governments and publics are predisposed to cooperate with it, without being bribed or threatened.

[C] The concept proved enormously influential. Governments that had never used the phrase began to talk about "nation branding", cultural diplomacy and global rankings of soft power. Scholarship programmes, international broadcasting, film industries and even national football teams were reframed as strategic assets. In one sense this was a vindication of Nye's argument; in another, it threatened to empty the concept of meaning. If everything that makes a country look good counts as soft power, the term risks becoming a synonym for reputation.

[D] Critics raise deeper objections. First, attraction is difficult to measure and harder still to link to specific outcomes. Admiring a country's music does not necessarily mean supporting its foreign policy; millions of people consume the culture of states whose governments they distrust. Second, much of a country's appeal lies outside the control of its government. Popular culture, independent universities and civil society generate attraction precisely because they are not instruments of the state; once they are openly deployed as tools of policy, they may lose the credibility that made them attractive. Nye himself acknowledged that soft power is harder for governments to wield than hard power, because so many of its resources are beyond their direct command.

[E] A further complication is that soft power can be squandered quickly. Policies perceived as hypocritical — preaching human rights while violating them, or championing free trade while practising protectionism — erode the very legitimacy on which attraction depends. In an age of instant global media, the gap between a country's professed values and its conduct is visible to audiences everywhere, and credibility, as Nye later observed, becomes the scarcest resource.

[F] None of this makes the concept useless. Its enduring value lies in drawing attention to the fact that legitimacy affects the cost of achieving one's goals. A state that is trusted needs fewer threats and fewer payments to gain cooperation. Soft power is best understood not as a separate instrument, to be used instead of military or economic strength, but as a condition that makes all forms of power cheaper — or, when it is lost, considerably more expensive.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: The price of attention: who profits when we keep scrolling?
standfirst: More than fifty years ago an economist warned that a wealth of information would create a poverty of attention. The digital economy has turned his warning into a business model.
paragraphs: [A] In 1971, long before smartphones or social networks, the economist and cognitive scientist Herbert Simon made an observation that now seems prophetic. In an information-rich world, he argued, information consumes something: the attention of its recipients. A wealth of information therefore creates a poverty of attention. The design problem of the future, Simon suggested, would not be how to supply more information, but how to help people decide what to ignore.

[B] Half a century later, the scarcity Simon described has become the basis of an entire economy. Many of the most widely used digital services are free at the point of use. Their revenue comes from advertising, and advertising pays for attention: the more time users spend on a platform, and the more precisely their interests can be predicted, the more valuable that platform becomes. In this sense, as critics often put it, the user is not the customer but the product being sold.

[C] This business model shapes design. Features such as infinite scrolling, autoplay, notifications and personalised recommendation feeds are not neutral conveniences; they are engineered to reduce the friction that might otherwise lead a user to stop. Recommendation systems learn which content holds each person's attention longest. Because emotionally arousing material — outrage, fear, novelty — tends to perform well on these measures, some researchers worry that platforms systematically amplify it, with consequences for public debate as well as for individual well-being.

[D] The evidence on harm is, however, contested. Studies of social media use and mental health have produced mixed results, and many associations are small. It is difficult to separate cause from correlation: anxious people may use their phones more, rather than phones making people anxious. Defenders of the platforms point out that users derive real value from them — information, connection, entertainment — and that "attention" has always been the currency of newspapers, radio and television, which also competed for audiences with dramatic headlines.

[E] What may be new is the scale and precision of the competition. A newspaper cannot rearrange its pages for each reader in real time; a feed can. Individual users face teams of engineers and data scientists whose explicit goal is to increase engagement, and the asymmetry of knowledge between the two sides is considerable. This is why some reformers argue that responsibility cannot rest on personal self-discipline alone, any more than healthy eating can be achieved purely through individual willpower in an environment saturated with cheap, heavily marketed food.

[F] Proposed responses vary widely. Some focus on regulation: limiting data collection, banning certain design features for children, or requiring platforms to offer feeds that are not driven by engagement. Others emphasise design ethics within the industry, or tools that help users set limits. Still others return to Simon's original insight: in an age of abundance, the scarce skill is not finding information but filtering it. Teaching that skill — deciding what deserves our attention — may be one of the central tasks of education in the twenty-first century.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: A table for one: the rise of living alone
standfirst: In many wealthy countries, one-person households are now common. Is this a sign of social decline, or of new kinds of freedom?
paragraphs: [A] For most of human history, living alone was unusual. People lived with parents, spouses, children, servants or lodgers, and households of one were largely confined to widows and a few eccentrics. Historical records suggest that this began to change in early-industrialised countries more than a century ago, and the shift accelerated in the second half of the twentieth century. Today, according to data compiled by Our World in Data, one-person households account for a large share of homes in many rich countries, and in some northern European cities they make up around half of all households.

[B] The pattern is closely linked to wealth. Across countries, the share of people living alone tends to rise with national income. This is not surprising: living alone is expensive. It requires an entire home's worth of rent, heating and furniture for a single person, as well as a labour market that offers stable incomes and a welfare state or pension system that reduces dependence on family. Where those conditions are absent, sharing a household is often an economic necessity rather than a preference.

[C] Demographic change has also played a role. People marry later, divorce more often and live longer than in the past. A widowed grandmother who would once have moved in with her children may now remain in her own flat for decades. Young professionals increasingly spend a period of their twenties or thirties living independently before or instead of forming a couple. Living alone, in other words, is less often a single permanent condition than a stage that many people pass through, sometimes more than once.

[D] It is tempting to read these figures as evidence of an epidemic of isolation. Commentators frequently cite the rise of solo living alongside warnings about loneliness, implying that one causes the other. Yet the relationship is far from straightforward. Loneliness is a subjective feeling: the gap between the relationships people want and the ones they have. Living alone is simply an arrangement. Many people who live by themselves have rich social lives and value the privacy and autonomy their homes provide, while others feel profoundly lonely in crowded family homes. Analyses of survey data have not found clear evidence that loneliness has risen in step with solitary living.

[E] This does not mean the trend is free of risks. Older people living alone may be vulnerable if their health declines, and those without close relatives can struggle to find support in a crisis. In poorer countries where welfare systems are weaker, a growing number of single-person households could place new pressures on families and states. Housing markets, too, have been slow to adapt: much of the existing housing stock was designed for families, and small, affordable homes are scarce in many cities.

[F] Perhaps the most interesting question is not whether living alone is good or bad, but what kinds of community it requires. If more people live by themselves, the importance of what sociologists call "third places" — cafés, libraries, sports clubs, community centres — increases. Cities that make it easy to be alone without being isolated may turn out to be the ones best prepared for the households of the future.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: When results won't repeat: science and the reproducibility debate
standfirst: Repeating an experiment and getting the same result is meant to be the foundation of science. A survey of researchers suggested it happens less reliably than the public assumes.
paragraphs: [A] Science depends on a simple promise: if you follow the same method, you should get the same result. A finding that only one laboratory can produce is, at best, a curiosity. Yet over the past two decades, attempts to repeat published studies in fields from psychology to cancer biology have frequently failed. The problem has become known as the replication crisis, or, more cautiously, the reproducibility debate.

[B] In 2016 the journal Nature published the results of an online survey of more than 1,500 researchers. Just over half agreed that there was a significant crisis of reproducibility, and a large majority reported that they had, at some point, failed to reproduce another scientist's experiment; many had even failed to reproduce their own. Yet the same respondents were not pessimistic about science as a whole. Most still trusted much of the published work in their field, and relatively few thought that a failed replication automatically meant the original result was wrong.

[C] This apparent contradiction makes sense once we look at the causes. Some failures to replicate have innocent explanations: an experiment may depend on subtle details of equipment, materials or technique that the original paper did not describe. Others reflect genuine weaknesses in how research is done. Respondents to the survey most often pointed to selective reporting and the pressure to publish. Studies with small samples and low statistical power are also more likely to produce results that look impressive by chance and then disappear when others try to repeat them.

[D] The incentives of academic careers can make these problems worse. Researchers are rewarded for publishing novel, positive findings in prestigious journals. A study that confirms someone else's result, or that finds nothing at all, is harder to publish and rarely advances a career. As a result, the published literature can over-represent striking findings, while the less exciting attempts that would put them in context remain unpublished in "file drawers".

[E] Over the past decade, many reforms have been proposed and tried. In pre-registration, researchers publicly state their hypotheses and analysis plans before collecting data, which makes it harder to change the question after seeing the results. Some journals now accept papers on the basis of their design rather than their findings, so that a well-planned study is published whether or not it produces an exciting result. Sharing data and code allows others to check analyses, and large collaborative projects repeat key experiments across many laboratories at once.

[F] It is worth stressing what the reproducibility debate does not show. It does not mean that science is unreliable in general, or that every surprising result is false. Self-correction is the method working as intended: findings are tested, some do not survive, and confidence is adjusted. The real risk lies elsewhere — in a culture that treats a single published study as settled fact, whether in a laboratory, a newsroom or a government department.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Who owns the past?
standfirst: Museums in Europe hold millions of objects taken from other parts of the world. Calls to return them raise difficult questions about history, ownership and identity.
paragraphs: [A] Walk through the galleries of almost any major European museum and you will encounter objects from distant places: sculptures, manuscripts, ceremonial masks, human remains. Some were bought or exchanged fairly. Many others were acquired during periods of colonial rule, military conquest or unequal trade, when the people who made or owned them had little power to refuse.

[B] For decades, museums defended their collections with two main arguments. The first was legal: objects had often been acquired under the laws of the time, and national legislation sometimes forbids museums from giving items away. The second was what might be called the universal museum argument: by displaying artefacts from many cultures side by side, large museums allow visitors to see human history as a shared story, and they have the resources to conserve fragile objects.

[C] Critics find neither argument convincing. Laws written by colonial powers, they point out, can hardly settle questions of justice. And the idea of a universal museum sits uneasily with the fact that most of the world's population will never visit the cities where these collections are kept. For communities whose sacred objects or ancestors' remains are on display abroad, the issue is not access to world culture, but respect and the right to tell their own history.

[D] In recent years, the debate has shifted. A number of governments and institutions have agreed to return specific items, including bronze sculptures, carved figures and human remains, to the countries or communities they came from. Some museums have begun detailed research into the provenance of their collections, tracing how each object arrived and whether it was obtained with consent.

[E] Return, however, is rarely simple. There may be disagreement about who the rightful owner is: a national government, a royal family, a local community or the descendants of the original makers. Some objects are fragile and require specialist conditions. In other cases, the countries of origin have chosen long-term loans or joint exhibitions rather than permanent return, at least for now.

[F] What the debate reveals is that museums are not neutral spaces. The decision about what to collect, how to label it and where to keep it reflects choices about whose history matters. Whatever happens to individual objects, that recognition may be the most lasting change of all.

author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)
title: Why false stories travel faster than the truth
standfirst: False claims often spread further online than accurate ones. Understanding why matters more than simply blaming technology.
paragraphs: [A] A large study of stories shared on a major social network, published in 2018, reached a striking conclusion: false news tended to spread further, faster and more widely than true news. Crucially, the researchers found that this was driven mainly by people rather than automated accounts. Humans, it seemed, were more willing to pass on falsehoods.

[B] One explanation is novelty. False stories are, almost by definition, more surprising than true ones, because they are not limited by what actually happened. Surprising information attracts attention and gives the person who shares it a kind of social reward: they appear well informed and first with the news. False stories also tend to provoke strong emotions such as fear, anger or disgust, and emotionally charged content is shared more often.

[C] Our own reasoning plays a part too. People are more likely to believe and share claims that fit what they already think, a tendency known as confirmation bias. When a story confirms our views about a group or a politician, we may not stop to check it. Repetition matters as well: hearing a claim several times makes it feel more familiar, and familiar statements are more easily mistaken for true ones.

[D] Platforms have tried a range of responses, including labelling disputed posts, reducing the visibility of content flagged by fact-checkers and removing accounts that spread coordinated campaigns. Each approach has drawbacks. Labels may be ignored, or even increase attention; removal raises concerns about censorship and about who decides what is true.

[E] Some researchers argue that the most promising approach is to change how people share rather than what they see. In experiments, simply asking users to think about whether a headline is accurate before sharing reduced the spread of false content. Others favour "prebunking": teaching people in advance about common manipulation techniques, such as fake experts or emotional language, so that they recognise them later.

[F] None of these solutions is complete. False information has existed as long as communication itself, and technology has mainly changed its speed and scale. The lasting defence may be less a technical fix than a habit of mind: pausing, checking and being willing to admit that a story we like might not be true.
